sourceTitle: When a Probability Becomes a Headline
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Advanced original Astronomy Reading test, expert content approval pending.

questions.q: What is the chief limitation of portraying planetary defence as a fight against a hostile universe?
choices: It makes astronomical objects appear too small for serious study.
It overstates the historical role of scientific institutions.
It replaces the slower work of evidence and preparation with a misleading drama.
It suggests that spacecraft can be designed without engineering.
questions.explanation: The introduction challenges the battle metaphor because it obscures measurement and planning.

questions.q: Why must proximity, hazard and impact probability remain separate ideas?
choices: They answer distinct scientific and policy questions and cannot be reduced to a single alarm.
Each refers to a different class of rock that cannot enter Earth's orbit.
They are quantities that cannot be compared under any circumstances.
None can be estimated using the observations currently available.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one argues that the distinctions are necessary for proportionate public decisions.

questions.q: How can a seemingly precise statistic still conceal a selection effect?
choices: The instrument may stop working after the probability is calculated.
A calculation must always refer to a future date rather than the present.
The asteroid may decide to change its orbit after observation.
The detected sample reflects which objects the survey was able to observe.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two stresses that a catalogue reflects observing conditions and missed objects.

questions.q: What is the force of the claim that precision and completeness are not synonyms?
choices: Precise values are inherently less useful than rough estimates.
A carefully calculated value may still omit part of the relevant population.
No observational method is capable of estimating an object's motion.
A longer observational record always increases the measured danger.
questions.explanation: The writer distinguishes exact-looking orbital values from the completeness of the detection catalogue.

questions.q: Why does the evolution of Apophis estimates matter to the article's argument?
choices: It proves that early probabilities are deliberately misleading.
It shows all near-Earth objects eventually become harmless.
It suggests that scientists should avoid studying visible asteroids.
It demonstrates how additional evidence can transform a perceived threat into research opportunity.
questions.explanation: The Apophis example shows substantial revision after further measurements.

questions.q: What could readers reasonably learn from the early Apophis headlines?
choices: An initial probability is not a permanent verdict and may be revised decisively.
Scientists always predict a collision before locating an asteroid.
A later safe approach proves earlier observations were fabricated.
A close flyby is necessarily more dangerous than a direct collision.
questions.explanation: The account contrasts initial alarms with later evidence ruling out impact.

questions.q: Which generalisation would exceed what the DART result establishes?
choices: A kinetic collision can alter a tested asteroid's orbital period.
Future interventions depend on structure, trajectory and warning time.
One successful experiment guarantees a solution for every asteroid.
Early detection is essential to making a planned response useful.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph explicitly rejects treating DART as an all-purpose shield.

questions.q: Why might early small deflection matter more than late large intervention?
choices: A distant asteroid has less gravity than a nearby one.
An early alteration has more time to shift the object's eventual position.
Later interventions require less precise measurements.
A spacecraft always travels faster if it launches years in advance.
questions.explanation: The engineering argument stresses adequate warning and a modest change applied early.

questions.q: What complicates public investment decisions about rare asteroid disasters?
choices: There is no way to compare any public spending priorities.
All prevention measures provide immediate visible benefits.
Only scientific organisations can make political resource choices.
Costs are immediate while successful prevention may remain largely invisible.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph presents competing priorities and invisible benefits as a policy difficulty.

questions.q: According to the conclusion, what should be a central test of scientific authority?
choices: Whether institutions revise assumptions openly and sustain systems that tolerate correction.
Whether institutions promise absolute protection from every possible event.
Whether estimates remain unchanged after the first announcement.
Whether the most dramatic interpretation attracts public interest.
questions.explanation: The conclusion privileges inspectable assumptions, revisions and reliable institutions over certainty claims.
